items.title: Newer Rigol Scopes Get a Custom Linux Firmware
items.summary: Electronics test equipment is a topic near and dear to many Hackaday readers. The average reader of this article is most likely within 50 feet of a multimeter, and it wouldn’t be much of a surprise to find they own multiple oscilloscopes. [dekajoule] has been working on a new firmware for the DHO series of Rigol oscilloscopes, the OOS (Open Operating System) . The DHO series of Rigol oscilloscopes was released in 2022. This series followed the very popular 1000Z series, which we’ve featured before in hacks that unlock built-in capabilities from budget oscilloscopes. The OOS project that [dekajoule] has been working on is similar, but maybe even more exciting, as it gives you even greater control over the scope. OOS runs on the built-in SD card that comes with the DHO scopes, and better still it can run alongside the existing OS, allowing you to swap back to the original OS if you decide to. There are a few different ways to install OOS, ranging from opening up the scope and cloning the SD card to using ADB over the network. This project is still relatively new and as such it’s only been tested on a couple of models, but if the community support for the 1000Z series scopes is any indication, there are likely no shortage of users who would be interested in getting a little more out of their scope. items.title: A 3D Printed Pixel Clock, with a Twist
items.summary: The availability of cheap addressable RGB LED strips has been a huge boon for hardware hackers, as it makes many projects far more accessible. This usually requires a lot of snipping, followed by the monotony of connecting up a bunch of fiddly jumper wires, but that’s still generally preferable to having to solder all of the LEDs individually. But what if you didn’t even have to do that? That was the goal of the brilliantly designed PixelClock by [Dom Dominici] — by carefully weaving a continuous 2.5 meter strip of WS2812B LEDs through its 3D printed structure, you can create a 7×19 display without any tedious manual work. Technically you do “waste” a few LEDs in the process since they’ll be on the inside of the folded strip, but that’s literally and figuratively a small price to pay for the added convenience offered by this approach. We saw this one in person during Hackaday Supercon, and [Dom] tells us the whole idea was to make it as accessible as possible for new players. While we know there’s plenty of readers who actually enjoy the process of stripping and soldering wires, that’s not necessarily true for the average person. Of course the builder still needs to connect the end of the LED strip to the ESP32 WROOM development board that controls it, but that’s still a lot less intimating of a prospect for somebody that doesn’t breathe solder smoke on the regular. The PixelClock is configured via a web interface running on the ESP32, so there’s nothing you need to install on your phone or computer to get it working. items.title: The Fastest Paddleboard in the World
items.summary: The world is full of linguistic boundaries that seem obvious during regular communication but can break down upon closer inspection. Is a pizza an open-faced sandwich? Is an ebike a motor vehicle? Are palms actually trees? Is a certain number of grains of sand a heap? Without diving too much into the world of philosophy, we might all at least agree that strapping 12 kW of motors to a paddleboard might turn it into another type of vehicle entirely, likely without the word “paddle” in its name. But either way, this is likely the fastest craft of its kind in the world . Many other types of vessel of this type use off-the-shelf motor kits with shrouds, exposed bolts, and other drag-maximizing features. [rctestflight] has a lot of experience building custom watercraft without these downsides and figured he could put together something a little more hydrodynamic. His paddleboard incorporates two masts from a previous hydrofoil build , as well as two six kilowatt electric motors positioned at the end of each one. With some batteries in a waterproof case and a remote control to command them, the paddleboard quickly gets up on plane provided the rider is in the appropriate forward position. For anyone familiar with [rctestflight]’s builds, you’ll know this isn’t just someone who slaps a motor onto a piece of fiberglass and tosses it into a lake. A lot of work went into this build, including some propellers that were developed during a long series of tests to find ideal propeller shapes for various applications. With all of the tuning done it travels across the surface of the water in excess of 40 kph, much faster than any other “paddle” board we’ve seen before. items.title: Water in the Ancient Desert
items.summary: The desert of the Iranian Plateau receives very little rainfall, and most of it falls in the mountains before flowing underneath the porous ground of the region. The ancient Persians figured out a way to access the water and build a flourishing civilization in the desert . Half a million vertical shafts cover the Iranian Plateau and are evidence of the massive hydraulic engineering project that allowed cities to thrive in this hostile climate. Persian mathematician Al-Karaji helpfully wrote the book on the method, called The Extraction of Hidden Waters. After examining the land for clues, a piece of wool on a string was lowered in hole, and if it came back wet, a series of test wells were drilled until you found water. Dropping approximately 1 m for every 1 km, the tunnel, or qanat, would then be dug from the outlet where the water level is even with the surface back to the mother well where the water was discovered. A crew of four muqanni worked digging the tunnel between vertical shafts spaced about 30 m apart and kept an eye on oil lamps that could warn them of oxygen-deprived air much like coal miner lamps in more recent times. Once the water was at the surface, a complex series of channels and administration made sure crops were irrigated, public baths were supplied, and drinking water was secured for everyone. There was also water storage for dryer seasons and even the ability to make and store ice despite the lack of electricity. items.title: Can’t Get the Right Cassette Mechanism? Have a Go at Making Your Own!
items.summary: In the world of cassette tape enthusiasts, it’s an oft-repeated factoid that there is only one tape deck mechanism still being manufactured. The truth may be a tiny bit murky on that front, but it’s certain that cassettes are no longer a mainstream medium. So we’re bowled over by [Svofski], who’s creating his own cassette mechanism from scratch . The mechanism takes the form of a chassis made from PCBs, and with each spindle powered by a separate brushless motor. There doesn’t appear to be a capstan — instead it uses an optical mouse sensor to sense tape speed and thus provide input for motor control. As we understand it, this thing is designed to have more in common with a data backup tape drive than an audio player. Thus before any cassette fans become too excited it’s worth tempering that enthusiasm. The project in hand is to make a data tape drive rather than a linear cassette player, so while it is a cassette mechanism, it isn’t as it stands one you’d use for audio. And as he explains at length in his GitHub repository and a set of videos , it’s not there yet. But the mere fact of its existence is deeply impressive, and we think you’ll agree. The most recent video of the series is below. It was used as a datasette quite a few times in the 1980s and has/had better tape transport, maybe. After all, it was used for a serious application, dictation devices. Systems using it were, for example, the Sharp PC-1500 pocket computer (its expansion unit) or that FS-9600 datasette drive for C64. Key principles include aligning reduction and output dimensions to 256 for systolic arrays, adopting LatentMoE to compress routed token traffic, and mapping parallel axes directly onto physical links.

items.title: Securing Your Agents: A Hands-On Guide to Agent Anomaly Detection
items.summary: This guide walks developers through setting up Agent Anomaly Detection on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform to monitor AI agent telemetry and catch behavioral risks. It demonstrates how to deploy a sample customer support agent, trigger out-of-scope security findings, and configure proactive alerts using Cloud Monitoring and Security Command Center.

items.title: Agents are sessions, not requests: size GKE node pools for AI agent sessions
items.summary: AI agent sessions remain active and idle for most of the workday, making traditional one-Pod-per-session allocations inefficient for cluster resources. By using open-source tools like Agent Substrate and AX on GKE, developers can park idle sessions in object storage to release compute resources while maintaining session state. This approach optimizes resource utilization and reduces Kubernetes node costs by up to 40%.

items.title: How Agent Anomaly Detection scores on benchmarks we didn't write
items.summary: Agent Anomaly Detection (AAD) provides asynchronous, low-latency monitoring for AI agents by analyzing OpenTelemetry traces and logs to flag goal hijacks and tool misuse. Tested across five public security benchmarks, AAD successfully caught 87% of harmful instructions carried out by agents without adding runtime latency. Developers can integrate AAD alongside semantic governance and strict tool limits as part of a defense-in-depth strategy to secure agentic applications.

items.title: Catch Go bugs that fuzzing misses with Gemini and a constraint solver
items.summary: How pairing Go's surviving compiler bounds-check traps with Gemini 4 Argon and the Z3 constraint solver catches latent out-of-bounds panics in Go code and uncovers a slice-capacity blind spot in go test -fuzz.

items.title: A2UI 1.0: Build delightful, fast, reliable, agentic experiences
items.summary: A2UI 1.0 is an open protocol for generative UI that enables AI agents to render interactive, native screens across web, mobile, and desktop applications. Developers can leverage open-source renderer SDKs—including React, Angular, Lit, Flutter, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose—alongside agent SDKs for Python, TypeScript, and Dart. The release introduces bidirectional function calls, swappable inference formats, and secure data binding to help teams seamlessly integrate generative UI into their product stacks.

items.title: On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery
items.summary: Google AI Edge Gallery now supports on-device, offline Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) capabilities for building developer-friendly voice applications. Developers can leverage ML Kit for optimized Android performance, or use MediaPipe Tasks and LiteRT for cross-platform open-weight model integration. This local pipeline seamlessly pairs lightweight speech models with on-device small language models like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 to enable real-time streaming transcription and low-latency synthesis.

items.title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism
items.summary: Google Cloud's MaxText framework now supports long-context training up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs by implementing four context-parallel strategies: All-gather, A2A, P2P, and USP. Powered by the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel, these strategies effectively manage attention compute and memory bottlenecks without materializing full key-value sequences in high-bandwidth memory. Developers can adopt these capabilities in MaxText v0.2.4 to achieve high Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) across large-scale model training workflows.

items.title: From prompt to app: Build with Google Maps in AI Studio
items.summary: Developers can now build applications powered by Google Maps Platform directly within Google AI Studio by prompting Gemini with real-world geospatial concepts. The integration eliminates traditional configuration hurdles by providing one-click demo keys that generate instantly without requiring Cloud Console redirects or credit cards. This setup grants developers immediate access to core APIs—including Maps, Places, and Routes—supported by daily sandbox quotas for seamless prototyping.

items.title: What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
items.summary: Pathways is a single-controller distributed training system designed to coordinate large-scale model training across multiple accelerator groups by representing computations as a global dataflow graph. Unlike traditional SPMD models like DDP and FSDP that rely on synchronous collectives, Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and a central scheduler to maximize hardware utilization and prevent deadlocks in complex workloads. By decoupling model definition from physical hardware via virtual devices, developers can efficiently scale complex training architectures and seamlessly handle dynamic workloads like reinforcement learning post-training.

items.title: Agent Distraction
items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. In 6% of encounters, agents act on these comments, with 83% being entirely unprompted by the developer. These detours result in significant overhead—adding 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session—split between chasing closed tickets (41%) and unauthorized scope creep on open bugs (57%). Higher-capability models show higher distraction rates, highlighting the need for automated cleanup and linters to maintain agent-friendly codebases

items.title: Fast, reliable A2UI, with swappable inference formats
items.summary: A2UI now supports swappable inference formats, introducing A2UI Express which uses up to 3x fewer tokens and cuts latency by compiling compact Python-style syntax into standard A2UI JSON via Agent SDKs. Developers can also use controlled generation with TypeSafe's Jev system-decision models to render known-shape screens in under 300 ms while smaller models stream text. These updates require no changes to frontend renderers or component catalogs, offering flexible performance levers for generative UI development across Python, TypeScript, and Dart.

items.summary: Google Workspace now offers native support for Markdown (.md) files, allowing developers and AI agents to seamlessly collaborate on documentation directly in Google Docs without manual file conversions. This integration preserves native file fidelity for use with Git repositories and developer tools while unlocking standard Docs features like line-level commenting, rendered Drive previews, and tracked version history.
